1o.planHtml:
Buy Order: #1 of 6 — Precon-first

In print, forgiving, and the deck the counters arc starts on.

How to buy it: Box now (~$45). First singles trip: Soul Warden, Pristine Talisman, Authority of the Consuls.

Bracket Placement: Bracket 2 — Core

Zero Game Changers, no two-card infinite combos, no mass land denial, no extra-turn chaining. Power sits at 'well-tuned precon': it wins through resilient combat math over many turns, not explosive ones. Same placement under the Felothar commander variant.

Dialing it up: This is the table's fair-and-forgiving deck — leave it at 2 for normal nights. The Top-of-Bracket-3 package below is the full send when you want it.

How to Play This Deck

Ramp with mana dorks and walls (Faeburrow Elder, Sylvan Caryatid, Axebane Guardian) into a board of high-toughness defenders. Land Betor, then attack, take damage, and gain life through combat and your lifegain creatures - Betor's +1/+1 counters land at your END STEP based on total life gained that turn, so the counters always arrive AFTER combat. Sequence: attack -> damage -> life gain -> end step -> counters land. Multiply those counters with Branching Evolution, Hardened Scales, and Ozolith, then spread them with Conclave Mentor, Evolution Sage, Karn's Bastion, Contagion Clasp, and Nesting Grounds. Hold Inspiring Call to protect your board through a wrath. Close games with Cathars' Crusade triggering off every creature you cast, turning your wall of defenders into attackers that end the game in a swing or two. Zero-dragon option: the box's second legend, Felothar the Steadfast (Human Warrior), runs this exact 99 as a toughness-combat commander — every creature deals damage equal to its toughness and your defenders can attack, which the deck already supports with Assault Formation in the 99. You give up Betor's lifegain-to-counters engine but gain a faster clock, a sacrifice-for-cards outlet, and a table with no dragon overlap at all.

Trackers & Counters Needed

TypeStatusNotes
+1/+1 countersNeededGlass gem counters or a dedicated dice set
-1/-1 countersNot UsedUse a visually different counter set than +1/+1
Poison / energy / experienceNot Used
Dry-erase life/commander-damage trackerNot UsedHeavy +1/+1 counter use (Betor's own trigger, Branching Evolution, Hardened Scales, Ozolith, Conclave Mentor, Evolution Sage) - bring 40-60 standard +1/+1 counters. No -1/-1 counters or poison in this deck. Standard life tracking (dice/app/pad) covers the lifegain swings.

Pros

  • Very forgiving to pilot - the counters/lifegain engine runs almost on autopilot
  • Extremely resilient board of high-toughness defenders that blocks nearly anything on the ground
  • Strong lifegain buffer against aggressive tables

Cons

  • Can be slow to close games without Cathars' Crusade or a big finisher online
  • Losing Betor to removal before the engine is protected is a real tempo hit
  • Ground-bound - evasive flying damage goes right through the wall

Strengths

  • High-toughness walls block almost anything on the ground
  • Multiple proliferate sources make counters snowball fast
  • Lifegain buys time against aggressive pods

Weaknesses

  • Vulnerable to board wipes if counters aren't protected (hold Inspiring Call)
  • Flying damage from Dragon/Angel decks goes around the wall entirely
  • A lot of durdling can happen before Betor is online and protected

2c.planHtml:
Buy Order: #5 of 6 — Commander-first

Atraxa is the deck and a third of its cost — buy her when the budget breathes.

How to buy it: Atraxa (~$31) and Command Tower first. Second trip: Contagion Engine, Karn's Bastion, Flux Channeler.

Bracket Placement: Bracket 2 — Core

Zero Game Changers in the main list, no two-card infinite combos, no mass land denial. Proliferate is powerful but slow and entirely self-contained.

Dialing it up: Leave it here for normal nights. The Top-of-Bracket-3 package below is the dial when you want max power.

How to Play This Deck

Ramp into Atraxa on turn four or five behind Fog Bank, Wall of Roots and Sylvan Caryatid. Land any counter source — a planeswalker, Forgotten Ancient, an Everflowing Chalice — and let the end-step proliferate compound it. Deepglow Skate is the convergence button: it doubles every counter on the board at once, which can ultimate a planeswalker out of nowhere. Karn's Bastion gives you a proliferate you can use even with Atraxa dead.

Trackers & Counters Needed

TypeStatusNotes
+1/+1 countersNeededGlass gem counters or a dedicated dice set
-1/-1 countersNot UsedUse a visually different counter set than +1/+1
Other trackingNeededcharge counters
Other trackingNeededloyalty counters
Dry-erase life/commander-damage trackerNeededHeavy counter use of several kinds at once — bring +1/+1 counters, charge counters for Everflowing Chalice and Astral Cornucopia, and a dry-erase for planeswalker loyalty.

Pros

  • Every trigger is upside for you and touches nobody else's board
  • Four colours means access to the best removal in the game
  • Atraxa's 4/4 flying deathtouch lifelink body defends by itself

Cons

  • Atraxa is a $31 card and the mana base needs care
  • Four colours on a budget means slower, taplandy mana
  • Without a counter source in play the commander does nothing

Strengths

  • Deathtouch plus lifelink makes attacking you a bad idea
  • Proliferate scales with anything — it never becomes a dead effect
  • Deepglow Skate is a genuine one-card convergence turn

Weaknesses

  • Colour-screw is the real failure mode, not removal
  • Slow to start — nothing meaningful happens before turn four
  • A planeswalker-heavy board draws attacks from the whole table

Play lands. Gitrog's end-step sacrifice draws you a card every turn even when nothing else is happening, and with Ramunap Excavator that sacrificed land comes straight back out of the graveyard. Dialing it up: Leave it here for normal nights. The Top-of-Bracket-3 package below is the dial when you want max power.

How to Play This Deck

Deploy cheap walls every turn. Before Arcades they are pure defence; each one still replaces itself once he is down. Land Arcades and every 0/6 on the board becomes a 6-power attacker with vigilance-like safety, because they were never going to attack anyway. Buy Order: #2 of 6 — Precon-first

In print, Keith-endorsed, and the commander is in the box.

How to buy it: Box now (~$37). First singles trip: Bag of Holding, Containment Construct, Sevinne's Reclamation.

Bracket Placement: Bracket 2 — Core

Token recursion with efficient removal and zero Game Changers in the 99. Skullclamp is the strongest card here and it is deliberately NOT on the Game Changers list — powerful, but Core-legal.

Dialing it up: Careful when dialing up: BOTH the Farewell alternate (under Winds of Abandon) and Ancient Tomb in the stretch list are Game Changers. Bracket 3 allows three TOTAL — the package below plus either of those would exceed it, so choose.

How to Play This Deck

1) Turns 1-3: ramp with Sol Ring, Arcane Signet, Mind Stone, Fellwar Stone, and Talisman of Conviction while dropping cheap value creatures (Charming Prince, Knight of the White Orchid) and holding up removal (Path to Exile, Swords to Plowshares, Portable Hole). 2) Turns 4-6: land Excava, the Risen Past (or Quintorius, History Chaser if you'd rather run the grindier value-engine build) and start attacking — every Excava swing reanimates a cheap creature/artifact/enchantment from your yard as an extra 1/1 flying Spirit, and Quintorius (kept in the 99 either way) turns any card leaving your graveyard into a 3/2 Spirit token, so your own recursion effects double as token generation. 3) Turns 7+: go wide in the air — Luminarch Ascension, Mentor of the Meek, and Elspeth, Sun's Champion keep the tokens and cards flowing, Lightning Greaves keeps your key pieces alive through removal, and Skullclamp turns any dying 1/1 Spirit into two fresh cards. Clear blockers with Winds of Abandon/Cast Out and win by out-flying the table — your opponents' removal spells mostly just feed the next Excava attack trigger.

Trackers & Counters Needed

TypeStatusNotes
+1/+1 countersNeededGlass gem counters or a dedicated dice set
-1/-1 countersNot UsedUse a visually different counter set than +1/+1
Other trackingNeededFinality counters (from Excava, the Risen Past — an exile-replacement marker, not a stat counter, placed on anything she reanimates)
Other trackingNeededQuest counters (from Luminarch Ascension, if added)
Dry-erase life/commander-damage trackerNot UsedThis deck only lightly touches +1/+1 counters (Spirit of Resilience, Augusta, and Luminarch Ascension's quest counters) and uses Excava's 'finality counter' as a rules marker. A small mixed bag of generic counter tokens or spare dice/beads covers it fully — Trey does not need a dedicated +1/+1 counter set, poison dice, or energy/experience trackers for this deck, and standard life-total tracking (phone app, d20, or pen and paper) is all that's needed beyond that.

Pros

  • Removal-resistant value engine — your own creatures dying often helps you by fueling the graveyard
  • Evasive win condition (flying Spirit tokens) that dodges most ground stalls
  • Cheapest entry point of every comparable Boros build researched — about $87 all-in versus $80-95 just for the sealed product on the fan-favorite Voltron/Auras alternatives
  • Reads completely differently than any deck already at Trey's table

Cons

  • Graveyard hate (Rest in Peace, Bojuka Bog, etc.) can shut off multiple engine pieces (Excava, Quintorius, Advanced Reconstruction, Primary Research) at once
  • Card draw leans on Skullclamp and recursion — protect the Clamp, because the deck 'draws' through combat and the graveyard more than raw card advantage
  • Many payoffs are 1-toughness tokens that die to incidental damage or edicts

Strengths

  • Graveyard resilience/recursion
  • Evasion via flying tokens
  • Efficient, low-cost upgrade curve
  • Distinct table identity

Weaknesses

  • Vulnerable to dedicated graveyard hate
  • Thin raw card draw
  • Board wipes cost tempo (though the deck recovers faster than most)
  • Fragile 1-toughness token bodies

6c.planHtml:
Buy Order: #6 of 6 — Singles-first, staged

The Capstone and the graduation exam — build it last, enjoy it longest.

How to buy it: Nethroi, Buried Alive, Fauna Shaman and the mill package (~$45). Craterhoof, Elesh Norn and Vigor are later trips.

Bracket Placement: Bracket 3 — Upgraded

Craterhoof plus mass reanimation is a genuine game-ending turn, and the deck carries premium payoffs. Still zero Game Changers in the main list — the three in the package take it to the Bracket 3 ceiling.

Dialing it up: Leave it here for normal nights. The Top-of-Bracket-3 package below is the dial when you want max power.

How to Play This Deck

Mill and trade for the first several turns: Stitcher's Supplier, Satyr Wayfinder and Grisly Salvage stock the graveyard while Wall of Blossoms and cheap removal keep you alive. Buried Alive puts exactly the three creatures you want in the yard. Then mutate Nethroi onto anything and return ten total power — Elesh Norn plus Karmic Guide plus a body, or Archon of Cruelty on its own. Craterhoof turns that returned board into lethal in the same turn.

Trackers & Counters Needed

+1/+1 countersNeededGlass gem counters or a dedicated dice set

Other trackingNeededmutate order tracking
Dry-erase life/commander-damage trackerNeededBring +1/+1 counters for Vigor, and a dry-erase card or sleeve marker to track which creature Nethroi is mutated onto and in what order.

Pros

  • One card converts twenty turns of quiet setup into a full board
  • White and green give the walls and clean answers Sultai never had
  • Luminous Broodmoth and Vigor make board wipes a bad trade for everyone else

Cons

  • Shares every graveyard deck's exposure to Rest in Peace
  • Nethroi mutating onto a creature can be answered in response
  • The most expensive deck of the six by a wide margin

Strengths

  • Deliberate setup — you choose what goes in the yard rather than hoping
  • Elesh Norn is both a payoff and a one-sided board wipe
  • Multiple mass-return effects, so Nethroi is not a single point of failure

Weaknesses

  • A single graveyard-hate permanent costs you the game plan
  • Very little pressure before the mutate turn
  • Three colours plus double-costed bombs is a demanding mana base

Stretch Cards — would improve the deck, but break this budget; each is selectable on the deck tab (green rows)
